title: Pṛthivyāpas tejo vāyur ākāśā: the purification of the elements and the sheaths
theme: The virajā offerings continue from the elements and the senses’ objects to the acts of mind, speech and body, the self, inner self and supreme self, short offerings to hunger and the creator, a casting-out of misfortune, and the five sheaths.

Bhāskara: «विपाप्मा विगतत्रिविधमलश्च» — rid of the threefold impurity

morphology.note: Nominative plural of ākāśa, ‘space’, in a list of elements otherwise singular (pṛthivī, tejaḥ, vāyuḥ) and plural (āpaḥ); the plural matches the plural verb śudhyantām.

A singular subject with the plural verb śudhyantām; the anonymous commentator explains: «प्रायःपाठात्सर्वत्र बहुवचनप्रयोगश्छान्दसः» — the plural throughout is Vedic usage, following the recurrent wording.
Dative in -āya from kṣutpipāsā (feminine), as printed; read as a Vedic or formulaic form.

Dative of viviṭṭi; Sāyaṇa derives it from √viṣ ‘pervade’ with ṭ for ṣ by Vedic licence: «छान्दसः षकारस्य टकारः». Bhāskara reads it as an imperative of the same root, ‘pervade!’: «विविट्टि व्याप्नुहि विश्वं विष्णुरिवेति भावः».
Sāyaṇa: kaṣa, the made world, + utka, ‘eager’: the Lord eager to create. Bhāskara reads ghaṣotka, from √ghas ‘devour’: the one who swallows the three worlds («घस्ल् अदने»).
Nominative form used as the object of nāśayāmi; the commentator glosses it with the accusative «अलक्ष्मीम्».
Nominative singular masculine of the s-stem virajas, ‘without rajas (dust, stain; the quality that drives to action)’. Bhāskara: «विरजा विरजस्कः».

translation.literal: May my earth, waters, fire, air, space be purified; may I become light, free of stain, free of evil. Svāhā. May my sound, touch, form, taste, smell be purified … Svāhā. May my acts of mind, speech and body be purified … Svāhā. [Freed] from conceits of hidden intent, may I become light, free of stain, free of evil. Svāhā. May my self be purified … Svāhā. May my inner self be purified … Svāhā. May my supreme self be purified … Svāhā. To hunger, svāhā. To hunger-and-thirst, svāhā. To the all-pervading, svāhā. To the maker of the verses, svāhā. To the one eager to make, svāhā. The stain of hunger and thirst, the elder [sister], Misfortune, I destroy. Ill-being and failure — all [these] drive out, [and] my evil. Svāhā. May my [self] made of food, of breath, of mind, of understanding, made of bliss — [my] self — be purified; may I become light, free of stain, free of evil. Svāhā.
translation.readable: May the elements in me — earth, water, fire, air and space — be made pure; may I become light, free of stain, free of wrong. Svāhā. May sound, touch, form, taste and smell be made pure … Svāhā. May what I have done in thought, word and body be made pure … Svāhā. Freed of hidden conceits, may I become light … Svāhā. May my self, my inner self, my highest self be made pure … Svāhā. To hunger, to hunger and thirst, to the all-pervading, to the maker of the verses, to the one eager to create: svāhā. I destroy the stain of hunger and thirst, Misfortune, the elder sister; drive out want and failure and every evil of mine. Svāhā. May the self made of food, of breath, of mind, of understanding and of bliss be made pure; may I become light, free of stain, free of wrong. Svāhā.

syntax: Fifteen formulas. Seven share the refrain of 10.65 (‘may my … be purified; may I become light … svāhā’) with a new subject each time; one (avyaktabhāvair ahaṅkārair …) replaces the subject with an instrumental of what one is to be freed from. Five are bare datives with svāhā. Then a first-person sentence (… nāśayāmy aham) and an imperative addressed to the deity (… nirṇuda me pāpmānam), and the last formula returns to the refrain with the five sheaths as subject.

ambiguities.topic: how the supreme self can be purified
ambiguities.note: The anonymous commentator raises it: «ननु परमात्मनो नित्यशुद्धत्वात्कथं तच्छुद्धिः प्रार्थ्यत इति चेन्न» — the supreme self is ever pure; how can its purification be asked? His answer: impurity means its not being recognised, owing to ignorance, and purity its being known as one’s own self: «अविद्यादोषवशेन परमात्मनोऽप्रतिमानमशुद्धिरित्युच्यते», «स्वात्मत्वेन प्रतिभानं शुद्धिरिति विशेषाङ्गीकारात्».
Sāyaṇa and Bhāskara derive both words differently (see morphology); both read them as names of the Supreme.

The Tirupati e-text adds ॐ स्वाहा after the bare datives; the base and the Ānandāśrama text lack it. Sāyaṇa (his 61) and Bhāskara (his 61) both comment on an ‘om svāhā’ formula in their recensions, so the addition may reflect a recension rather than a copying error.

metre.name: prose
metre.note: Prose formulas, except kṣutpipāsāmalaṃ jyeṣṭhām alakṣmīr nāśayāmy aham, an anuṣṭubh half-verse of 16 syllables. The fifteen printed lines count 30, 29, 27, 24, 21, 23, 23, 4, 7, 5, 7, 6, 16, 19 and 43 syllables.

beginner: This long anuvāka continues the purifying offerings of the one before. Each short formula names something to be made pure — the five elements the body is made of; sound, touch, form, taste and smell; whatever one has done in thought, word and body — and repeats the wish: may I become light, free of stain, free of wrong. Then come brief offerings to hunger and thirst and to names of the creator, a line driving out misfortune, pictured as the elder sister of the goddess of fortune, and finally the five ‘sheaths’ of the self known from the Taittirīya Upaniṣad, from the body made of food to the self made of bliss. Bhāskara places these among the offerings of renunciation. The edition reports that use and makes no claim about what the rite achieves.
analogy: Like the last pages of an inventory that move from the furniture to the foundations and end with the owner’s name.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It asks that the elements, the objects of the senses, the acts of mind, speech and body, the self, inner self and supreme self, and the five sheaths be purified, each time with the refrain ‘may I become light, free of stain, free of evil, svāhā’; it makes offerings to hunger, hunger-and-thirst, the all-pervading, the maker of the verses and the one eager to make; and it casts out the stain of hunger and thirst, Misfortune, want and evil.

commentary.q: How does Bhāskara group these formulas?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: As in 10.65, he gives each list an anuvāka of its own in his recension: the five objects of sense, «शब्दादिगन्धान्तपञ्चविषयशुद्धिः पञ्चपञ्चाशे»; the five elements, «पृथिव्याद्याकाशान्तपञ्चभूतशुद्धिः षट्पञ्चाशे»; the five sheaths, «अन्नमयाद्यानन्दमयान्तपञ्चकोशशुद्धिः सप्तपञ्चाशे». He reads viviṭṭi as ‘pervade the universe, like Viṣṇu’, «विविट्टि व्याप्नुहि विश्वं विष्णुरिवेति भावः», and kaṣotka as ghaṣotka, from the root of devouring, «घस्ल् अदने». The refrain he glosses once, where the series begins (his 51; see 10.65).

commentary.q: How does Sāyaṇa read the names of the Supreme?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: viviṭṭi is Brahman whose pervasion is complete, «विशेषेण विष्टिर्व्याप्तिर्यस्य ब्रह्मणस्तद्विविष्टिः», with ṭ for ṣ by Vedic licence, «छान्दसः षकारस्य टकारः»; kaṣa is the made world, «कष्यते क्रियत इति कषो नामरूपकर्मात्मकः कार्यप्रपञ्चः», and kaṣotka the Lord eager to make it.

commentary.q: What does the anonymous commentator say on the other formulas?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: He reads the acts as those of mind, speech and body, «मनोवाक्कायानां कर्माणि»; avyaktabhāvair ahaṅkāraiḥ as a wish to be freed from empty pride, «अहंकारैर्व्यर्थगर्वैर्विमुक्तो भूयासम्»; ātmā as the body, with the plural verb explained as Vedic usage, «प्रायःपाठात्सर्वत्र बहुवचनप्रयोगश्छान्दसः»; the bare datives as offerings to the deities the words name, «एतदादिवक्ष्यमाणपञ्चमन्त्रेषु लिङ्गोक्ता देवता हविर्भुजः»; ṛgvidhāna as the Supreme who brings forth the verses, «ऋचो विदधाति करोत्युत्पादयतीति ऋग्विधानः परमात्मा»; and Alakṣmī as the elder sister of Lakṣmī, «लक्ष्म्या ज्येष्ठामग्रजामलक्ष्मीरलक्ष्मीम्». See ambiguities for his answer to how the supreme self can be purified. On viviṭṭi and kaṣotka his wording runs close to Sāyaṇa’s.

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta school commentary on this anuvāka is in the edition’s sources. Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara reads the formulas as the offerings of one taking up renunciation, Sāyaṇa and the anonymous bhāṣya as purifications and offerings addressed to the Supreme; none argues a school position here. Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary is not in the sources. No school position is given.

parallels.note: The five sheaths of the last formula are those taught in the Taittirīya’s Brahmānandavallī, which ends the series with the self made of bliss; Bhāskara says they were explained at the passage beginning brahmavid āpnoti (TU 2.1).

contemporary.text: The list moves from what a person is made of (elements) to what reaches them (sense objects), what they do (acts of mind, speech and body), what they are (self, inner self, highest self), and how a person can be described in layers (the five sheaths). It is an old and systematic map of human experience. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: Of thought, word and deed, which do you find hardest to keep ‘clean’?
reflect.deeper: The anonymous commentator answers that the supreme self is ‘impure’ only in not being recognised. What changes if purification means recognition rather than removal?
reflect.practice: At the end of today, review one thing you did in thought, one in word and one in deed.

references.text: The anonymous bhāṣya is quoted from vishvAsa’s assembled page for this anuvāka: the blocks labelled सायण-टीका and the unlabelled comments between them, which form one running commentary. vishvAsa labels the blocks Sāyaṇa’s, but the page closes with the pariśiṣṭa bhāṣya’s own colophon, naming the 66th anuvāka of the bhāṣya on the Yājñikī Upaniṣad, where Sāyaṇa’s colophons name his Vedārthaprakāśa; their numbering in the 80-anuvāka count and their wording are the anonymous bhāṣya’s, so the edition files them as the anonymous commentator’s. Sāyaṇa is quoted only from his own numbered comments (his anuvākas 58 and 59; his 61 comments on an ‘om svāhā’ formula). For the first formula (the elements) the page gives only a link to the section page 51-57_virajA_vipApmA, which has not been imported; the objects of sense and the five sheaths have no comment on the page. Sāyaṇa’s own comments on those three formulas (his anuvākas 55–57) are on that section page.
The Ānandāśrama pariśiṣṭa text repeats several formulas and adds मे शुध्यन्तां after avyaktabhāvair ahaṅkāraiḥ; the Tirupati e-text adds ॐ स्वाहा. These are listed on the sources page.

flags.note: The collation leaves for review the Ānandāśrama text’s added मे शुध्यन्तां in the avyaktabhāvaiḥ formula, its doubled क्षुधे स्वाहा, and its reading of the kaṣotka line.

The computed concordance maps no Sāyaṇa or Bhāskara anuvāka here; by content Sāyaṇa’s 58, 59 (and 61 for the Tirupati ‘om svāhā’) and Bhāskara’s 55–59 (and 61) comment on this anuvāka. They are cited explicitly.
viviṭṭi and kaṣotka/ghaṣotka are derived differently by Sāyaṇa and Bhāskara; the text does not decide.
